references.text: Jesus says the same about joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, in the parable of the lost sheep: [ref:Luk 15:7|Luke 15:7]. Verse 10 repeats and reinforces this point in the context of the parable of the lost coin.

In the parable of the prodigal son, the same joy over a sinner who returns is emphasized: [ref:Luk 15:32|Luke 15:32] – "we ought to rejoice and be glad, for this brother of yours was dead and has come to life".
Jesus declares that he has come to call sinners to repentance, which underlies the joy angels have over one who repents: [ref:Luk 5:32|Luke 5:32].

Angels are described as ministering spirits sent out to serve those who will inherit salvation ([ref:Hebr 1:14|Hebrews 1:14]), which highlights the angels' concern for human salvation, just as they rejoice over a sinner's repentance.

At Jesus' birth, the angels praise God and proclaim peace among people ([ref:Luk 2:13-14|Luke 2:13-14]). The angels are active witnesses to God's plan of salvation, and their joy over repentance is an extension of this praise.

The prophet Isaiah calls the wicked to leave their way and turn to the Lord, who will show mercy ([ref:Jes 55:7|Isaiah 55:7]). Repentance is at the heart of what causes joy among the angels in Luke 15:10.

God declares through Ezekiel that he does not delight in the death of the wicked, but rather that they turn from their ways and live ([ref:Esek 18:23|Ezekiel 18:23]). God's own joy over repentance is reflected in the angels' joy.

Again, God confirms that he does not want the wicked to die, but that they turn from their ways and live ([ref:Esek 33:11|Ezekiel 33:11]). This divine attitude is the background for heaven's joy over repentance.

When the church in Jerusalem heard that even the Gentiles had received repentance leading to life, they praised God ([ref:Apg 11:18|Acts 11:18]). This shows the concrete joy over sinners' repentance, as Jesus describes it in Luke 15:10.
The Lord does not want anyone to perish, but that all should come to repentance ([ref:2 Pet 3:9|2 Peter 3:9]). God's patient desire for repentance is the reason heaven celebrates when it happens.

In the book of Job, the sons of God (angels) appear before the Lord ([ref:Job 1:6|Job 1:6]). The expression "before God's angels" (ἐνώπιον τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ θεοῦ) in Luke 15:10 reflects the image of angels gathered in God's presence.
